newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Afghan Taleban accused of using poison gas.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban accused of using poison gas.

text.p: Afghanistan's ousted government on Monday accused the radical Islamic Taleban militia of using poison gas last month in its successful drive to capture Kabul, the capital.

Addressing the General Assembly, the government's foreign minister Abdul Rahim Ghafoorzai, said eyewitnesses, including experienced military commanders, saw corpses of government troops bleeding from the nose and ear and without any bullet wounds or other signs of penetration on their bodies.

"It is the strong conviction of the Islamic State of Afghanistan that the foreign sponsors of the Taleban have provided them with some type of internationally-banned gas or chemical weapons, used in the onslaught for the capture of Kabul," he said.
He said he personally saw the transcript of a recorded radio message between Taleban commanders on Sept. 11.

It said, in part, that new weapons had been brought from Pakistan to Kandahar. "You should immediately send these arms, which are gas weapons, through Torkham toward Nagarhar. Because we have organised a group of Taleban with special gear and are waiting for the said weapons. We can capture a large area with a single round," the minister alleged.
U.N. officials said they had seen no reports on chemical weapons used in Afghanistan.

Taleban, which dominates more than half the country, has applied for international recognition of its regime. But a U.N. credentials committee has not ruled on the application so Ghafoorzai was able to represent his government, which has fled to Taloqan in the northern province of Takhar.

Ghafoorzai said the Taleban, once a group of religious students, had its own reactionary interpretation of Islam, and was bent destroying modern science, museums, technology and take the country back to the dark ages.
"The Taleban, who still believe the earth is flat, are not the people for Afghanistan, not when we are about to enter the 21st century," he said.

He said the world community had forgotten Afghanistan and had not heeded appeals his government had made over the past years. Rather, the United Nations appointed an envoy instead of organising a mission of interested states to curb the Taleban before it captured more territory, he said.

"I must say this is the time to look back and see who is responsible for the ongoing human tragedy in Afghanistan?" he said. "Was it not the lack of any appropriate response by this organisation to the intransigent attitude of the Taleban that encouraged and enabled them to see the tunnel wide open and to pursue their designs?"
"The Islamic State of Afghanistan" he said, referring to his coalition government, "continuously warned the United Nations about the possible outcome."
"Mr. President, one thing manifest by the indifference thus far, is that Afghan blood is not cheap (but) worthless."
